opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the places where the machine learning community has been a bit too narrow. We've tended to treat uncertainty as a property of a single agent — a model has a posterior, or a confidence interval, or a calibrated probability, and then it acts. That's the classical decision-theoretic picture, and it's fine as far as it goes. But most consequential decisions aren't made by a single agent in isolation. They're made in markets, among many participants who have their own information, their own incentives, and their own uncertainties.

Once you're in an economic context, a few things change. First, uncertainty isn't just something you reduce by collecting more data; it's something other agents may have resolved better than you, and they may or may not want to share it. So there's information asymmetry, and that's the core of contract theory and mechanism design. If I'm a regulator, say the FDA, and a drug company knows more about their candidate drug than I do, my statistical test isn't just an inference problem anymore. It's a game. The company decides whether to run a trial based on what they believe, and my threshold for approval shapes who shows up. You have to design the inference procedure with incentives in mind.

Second, uncertainty quantification becomes something that has to be credible to other parties. That's partly why I've been enthusiastic about things like conformal prediction: you get guarantees that don't depend on believing someone's model is correct. In a multi-agent setting, that kind of distribution-free, verifiable guarantee matters a lot, because nobody has to trust your prior.

Third, there's the question of scarcity and competition. In recommendation systems, everyone being recommended the same restaurant is a problem; there are congestion effects. Uncertainty about preferences interacts with matching and allocation. Bandit algorithms in a market look different from bandits in isolation, because when you explore, you're affecting other people, and they're learning about you too.

So my broad view is that we should stop thinking of AI as an oracle that hands down decisions under uncertainty, and start thinking of it as part of a collective system — something closer to an economy, where learning, incentives, and uncertainty are all intertwined. Statistics, economics, and computer science each have a piece of that, and the interesting research is at the intersection.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that in a lot of machine learning the word "uncertainty" gets used in a rather narrow way. You have a predictor, you want a confidence interval or a calibrated probability, and the implicit picture is one agent, one objective, trying to get the right answer. That's the statistician's picture, and I've spent much of my career inside it. But it's not the picture that matters for most of the systems we're actually building.

Once you're in an economic context, there's no single decision maker. There are many agents, they have different information, different preferences, and critically, they respond to what you do. So uncertainty is no longer just a property of the world that you're trying to estimate away. It's a property of a system of interacting people, and some of it is strategic. If I'm a platform recommending restaurants, and I send everyone to the restaurant I'm most confident is good, I've created a crowd, and now it isn't good anymore. My "correct" prediction was undermined by the collective response to it. The uncertainty you should care about there is not "how sure am I about the quality of this restaurant" but "what happens to everyone when a lot of people act on the same information?"

And that changes how uncertainty should guide decisions in a few ways. One is that you want to reveal uncertainty rather than hide it. Markets have known this for centuries. Prices are, in a sense, uncertainty made visible, aggregated across many people who each know a little bit. A good market mechanism doesn't need any one participant to have the right answer. It needs the signals to flow so that scarcity, demand, risk, all of that shows up in a form people can act on. A lot of our AI systems do the opposite. They collapse everything into a single recommendation and present it with far more confidence than is warranted.

Another is that in an economic setting, uncertainty has a price, and the question of who bears it becomes central. If I hand you a prediction and you act on it and it's wrong, who pays? In classical decision theory that's just the loss function, but in a real system there's a distribution of winners and losers, and the design question is how to allocate risk so that people are willing to participate at all. That's what insurance does, what contracts do, what incentives do. I think we should be thinking about machine learning systems as mechanisms in that sense, where part of the design is deciding how uncertainty is shared, not just how it's quantified.

And the last thing I'd say is about the time horizon. In the single-agent view you make a decision, you see the outcome, you update. In an economy the feedback is slow, it's noisy, and it comes through other people's behavior, which changes the data you'll see next. So you have to be humble about the limits of learning from the data you happen to have, and you have to build in mechanisms that are robust to being wrong, rather than mechanisms that assume you'll converge to the truth. Decentralized systems have that kind of robustness partly because no one is relying on a single estimate. That's the lesson I keep coming back to: the goal isn't a system that is certain, it's a system where many uncertain agents can nonetheless coordinate and produce something good collectively.

astra-6.text:
An economic context makes you ask: uncertainty about what, and for whom? In a prediction problem, you might quantify uncertainty and then choose an action that minimizes some expected loss. But in an economic setting, that loss depends on other people’s decisions. They’re learning, they have their own information, and they respond to what you do.

Take a recommendation system. You could be quite certain that a particular restaurant is the best choice for each person. But if you send everybody there, it becomes congested, and your predictions cease to describe the experience people actually have. The decision changes the world you were predicting.

So uncertainty has to be considered alongside incentives, capacity, and the way decisions are coordinated. Who bears the cost of an error? Who benefits from gathering more information? Can a price or some other signal help people coordinate without requiring everyone to know everything?

That shifts the focus from making an isolated predictor more accurate to designing a system in which people can make good decisions together. Statistical uncertainty remains essential, but it’s one part of that larger problem.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, in an economic context, uncertainty isn’t just about whether my prediction is correct. It’s about what I should do, given that other people are making decisions too, and that our decisions affect one another.

Suppose I’m building a system that recommends routes to drivers. I might have uncertainty about the travel time on each road. But if I send everybody down the road that looks best, I change its travel time. So the uncertainty isn’t simply something out there that I measure and then act on. My actions help create the environment in which the predictions will be evaluated.

That means we have to think about costs, incentives, information, and feedback. Who bears the cost of an error? Who has information that I don’t have? Can we design an interaction that makes it worthwhile for them to reveal it? And how much exploration is appropriate when the benefits and costs fall on different people?

So I’d move away from the idea that we first quantify uncertainty and then attach a decision rule. We need to design the learning process and the economic interaction together. A confidence interval can be useful, but it doesn’t, by itself, tell you how to coordinate a collection of people with different objectives.
